items.title: Fighting paused in Ukrainian city under deal announced by Melania Trump
paras: Kyiv residents have been demanding help for the people of Oleshky. ( Reuters: Alina Smutko )
A regional truce between Russia and Ukraine is in effect in order to establish a humanitarian corridor for the city of Oleshky.
Melania Trump announced the truce last week, saying civilian officials would provide aid to residents and help them leave if they wished.
US-mediated talks between Russia and Ukraine are set to resume next month.
A ceasefire brokered with the assistance of Melania Trump has come into effect in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky.
Both sides said they would observe the truce, which began on Tuesday at 3am, local time, to allow for the establishment of a humanitarian corridor.
In a Telegram post, the Russian defence ministry said it had halted shelling in the direction of the city of Kherson, which faces Oleshky across the Dnipro River.
Ukrainian negotiator and parliamentary human rights commissioner Dmytro Lubinets said on social media that his country was "honouring its commitments".
He said the deal was reached with the help of the US first lady and the cooperation of Russian human rights commissioner Yana Lantratova.
The city, on the southern bank of the Dnipro River, was seized by Russian troops in 2022.
The population of Oleshky has dropped from about 24,000 before the Russian invasion in 2022 to about 2,000 today, including as many as 50 children, according to Ukrainian and US estimates.
Earlier this year former residents told AFP that those still in the city were hunting pigeons or subsisting on whatever they had in their garden.
The city was heavily damaged by the 2023 destruction of the Kakhovka dam, which unleashed major flooding along the Dnipro River.
The ceasefire comes as the Ukraine war grinds through its fifth year and ahead of the resumption of peace talks between Washington, Moscow and Kyiv next month.
None of the parties have said who will monitor the truce, or given details about the humanitarian operation set to accompany it.
"Residents who wish to evacuate will receive coordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination. I anticipate some will want to go to Russia and some to Ukraine," she said.
US cable network Newsmax says it has been granted "exclusive television access" to accompany observers entering the city later this week.
On Tuesday morning, the Ukrainian air force command issued nearly a dozen messages warning of ballistic missiles fired toward the capital.
Mayor Vitaly Klitschko said a strike hit the Southern Bridge -- one of Kyiv's main bridges -- and damaged its metro infrastructure.

items.title: Greens launch $21-a-week tax cut in bid to 'replace Labor'
paras: David Shoebridge will address the National Press Club on Wednesday. ( ABC News: Callum Flinn )
David Shoebridge will propose a $21-a-week tax cut for all taxpayers and an equivalent welfare boost in a speech at the National Press Club.
The Greens say the tax cuts could be paid for by taxing gas and other resources, but those policies have not been formally costed.
The new Greens leader is pursuing sharper differentiation with Labor, but his first few weeks have been derailed by allegations against senator Jordon Steele-John.
The Greens have called for a $21-a-week tax cut for all taxpayers and a welfare boost, in the party's first major policy launch since its new leader vowed to "replace Labor".

David Shoebridge, whose first weeks in the role have been derailed by allegations against Greens senator Jordon-Steele John, will front the National Press Club on Wednesday to launch a tax policy to "turn the tide" on inequality.
The new proposal would raise the tax-free threshold from $18,200 to $26,000 for all personal income taxpayers, a tax cut of up to $1,092 a year or $21 a week.
It would also add the same amount to all income support payments, including the JobSeeker unemployment benefit, student and carer payments, and the Age Pension.
"No matter who you are, whether you're working, studying, looking for work or on a pension, you'll get more," he will say, according to an extract of a speech seen by the ABC.

The policy would cost the budget $22 billion each year, according to the independent Parliamentary Budget Office (PBO). Senator Shoebridge will propose the cost be offset by collecting "rivers of gold" from gas and mining companies.

Some Greens insiders have framed the new leadership as an opportunity to reinvigorate the minor party, with published opinion polls suggesting minimal gain on the 12 per cent primary vote it recorded in the 2025 election, when it lost three lower house seats.
Greens parliamentarians were divided on how to interpret that loss, with some advocating a more constructive relationship with Labor, and others urging sharper differentiation.

Richard Denniss, whose left-wing think tank The Australia Institute is influential in Greens circles, wrote that former leader Larissa Waters was not "shouty" enough and had too much "nuance and subtlety" to cut through.
Richard Denniss (pictured) was critical of David Shoebridge's predecessor, Larissa Waters. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts )

Senator Shoebridge's claim he would "replace Labor" was seen as a decisive shift from his predecessor, and social media ads featuring deputy Steph Hodgins-May appear modelled on the approach of left-wing politicians in the United States and the United Kingdom.

But allegations of inappropriate behaviour towards women by Senator Steele-John, which he denies, have disrupted the reset, as have reports of a disagreement over Ukraine policy with leadership rival Sarah Hanson-Young.

The press club speech will focus on economic policy, although key details have not yet been fully fleshed out. The Greens's proposal for a 25 per cent gas export tax, adapted from The Australia Institute, has not been costed by the PBO.
Senator Shoebridge will use a figure by The Australia Institute, which suggested a gas tax could raise $17 billion a year.

A related proposal to apply a progressive royalties regime to mining has fewer details. Senator Shoebridge will claim the Greens "would raise" $28 billion from the tax, citing a report from the research organisation Prosper Australia.

But that figure is a ballpark calculation of how much state governments could raise if they all taxed royalties as much as Queensland does. The only federal tax canvassed by the report is offshore petroleum.

Senator Shoebridge's speech extract refers to a "Commonwealth tax" but does not specify which resources it would cover or how it would interact with state royalties, details a Greens source said were still to be determined.
The PBO also noted that the proposed welfare boost "may discourage [some] recipients from working additional hours" because of the way it is structured.

The Greens do not propose to means-test the $1,092 stipend, but the welfare payments themselves would remain means-tested. That means recipients would lose the full $1,092 all at once when they cross over the eligibility threshold for their welfare payment.

items.title: Mining giants lead ASX higher, banks and retailers fall, the Star soars

Share A A A The Australian sharemarket had a muted start but finished firmly in the green thanks to a rally by copper giants BHP and Rio Tinto, while a strong lead from Wall Street following the IPO filing of Anthropic benefited the tech sector.

The S&P/ASX 200 rose 40.2 points, or 0.5 per cent, to 8850.10, bouncing back after a weak morning, although seven of its 11 industry sectors remained in the red. It had added 0.2 per cent on Monday. The Australian dollar was trading at US70.20¢.

Anthropic’s IPO filing gave tech stocks on Wall Street a boost and helped lift the local market. Bloomberg Losses by banks and consumer stocks weighed on the local market, while the nation’s largest miners and parts of the tech sector advanced on the global AI trade. Energy stocks were mixed.

Star Entertainment shares rallied 13 per cent after the casino operator said its earnings in the September quarter swung back into the green, rising $25 million to $12 million, as revenues at its casinos increased and it slashed corporate costs. In a sign of a recovery from its crisis, the Star forecast its first positive annual operating cash flow for the first time in two years.

Mining stocks were fuelled by the sector’s two biggest stocks, BHP and Rio Tinto, which jumped 4.3 per cent and 2.5 per cent respectively. The copper heavyweights are often seen as a proxy for the AI trade, with investments in the technology driving demand for the red metal used in data centres and power infrastructure.

Gold miners Northern Star (up 2.1 per cent), Evolution Mining and Newmont (both up 1 per cent) ticked higher, with gold holding near $US4000 an ounce as traders prepared for a Federal Reserve decision this week that’s expected to keep interest rates in the world’s largest economy steady. Silver miner South32 climbed 2.6 per cent.

Amid local tech stocks, Codan – which makes components for drones used in the wars in the Middle East and Ukraine – rose 2.6 per cent. Embattled AI data centre operator NextDC climbed 3.8 per cent after its $3 billion share sell-off last week. Data centre and cloud networks provider Megaport rallied 9.6 per cent. However, software makers WiseTech Global (down 0.6 per cent), Xero (down 1.3 per cent) and Technology One (down 2.5 per cent) were all lower.
AI data centre owner Goodman Group pushed the property sector into the green, gaining 3.2 per cent gain.
All the Big Four banks declined, weighing down the wider market, with CBA down 0.7 per cent, Westpac down 1 per cent, NAB losing 1.7 per cent and ANZ Bank edging down 0.1 per cent.

Consumer stocks also struggled amid rising bets for another demand-sapping interest rate rise when the Reserve Bank meets again next week, with rates having risen already four times to a record high this year.

Inflation data to be released on Wednesday is expected to confirm ongoing price pressures for household essentials, prompting a further interest rate hike from the Reserve Bank when it meets on November 2 and 3. The RBA’s deputy governor warned last week that mortgage holders and businesses that the bank is facing “hard choices” in its bid to bring down inflation amid warnings it risks pushing the country into recession.

The nation’s largest retail stock, Wesfarmers, ended down 0.3 per cent, electronics chain JB Hi-Fi dropped 1.4 per cent, car seller Eagers Automotive shed 4.7 per cent, furniture retailer Harvey Norman fell 1.7 per cent and Rebel sport stores owner Super Retail Group dropped 1.8 per cent. Supermarket chain Coles slipped 0.7 per cent and dairy producer A2 Milk lost 2.7 per cent. Department store Myer’s shares slumped 4.8 per cent.

In the energy sector, oil and gas major Woodside added 0.3 per cent after selling its operating interest in the long-stalled Greater Sunrise liquefied natural gas project to a Timor-Leste state-owned company. The sale of the 33.44 per cent stake is worth as much as $US200 million ($284 million), it said, although most of that depends on the project being built. Santos edged up 0.1 per cent.

The price for a barrel of Brent crude slipped back below $US115 as stepped-up diplomatic efforts strengthened expectations that a broader escalation in the US-Iran war may be averted, though remains near the high end of its range since the war with Iran began. The highest price for the fossil fuel since then is nearly $US120, reached in March. Meanwhile, coal miners gained, with Yancoal up 1.6 per cent and Whitehaven Coal gaining 1.4 per cent.
On Wall Street overnight, US stocks climbed as investors digest Anthropic’s filing for its initial public offering and look ahead to key big tech earnings this week.

A news ticker displaying Anthropic’s IPO news on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange on Monday. Bloomberg The S&P 500 rose 0.7 per cent and more than recovered its losses from last week. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 0.3 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite closed 0.8 per cent higher.
Anthropic filed for its long-awaited market float, a landmark moment in the artificial intelligence industry that is growing ever hungrier for cash to power ahead.

The company behind Claude expects to begin trading on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol ANT, a filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission showed. Anthropic filed confidentially in June for a listing.

Investors are telling bankers on the deal that their estimate of a fair valuation has shifted down to around $US1.4 trillion to $US1.5 trillion after the company’s investor day, according to people familiar with the matter. A valuation of closer to $US1.75 trillion is potentially achievable, some of the people said, asking not to be identified as the information isn’t public.

Microsoft closed 1.5 per cent higher after it announced it will offer buyouts to about 60,000 workers, part of the company’s efforts to trim costs and retool its workforce for the artificial intelligence era.

The strongest lift for the market came from Nvidia, which rose 2.4 per cent. That helped the chip company recover some of its drop from three straight losing weeks, its longest such streak since June, and maintain its position as the largest stock on Wall Street above Apple.

But stocks elsewhere in artificial intelligence remained unsettled. They’ve been swerving on worries about whether their industry’s boom is under threat because of how expensive it’s become for companies to borrow money to build data centres and buy more AI chips.
Stocks are recovering their losses from last week ahead of a number of earnings reports this week from big companies, including Amazon and Intel.

Meta Platforms bounced up and down after outlining plans to raise $US35 billion by selling stock to help pay for its AI investments. It also said it could raise another $US60 billion by selling shares of a new class of its stock once it begins trading. Meta’s stock initially dropped more than 2 per cent, but it quickly flipped to a gain and then pulled back to a loss of 1.9 per cent.

Meta said Nvidia, Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom have already indicated they may buy a total of $US5 billion of stock in its offering. That’s a signal of strong interest from big chip companies that stand to benefit from additional AI investments. But it also gives fuel to critics of “circular financing” who say it raises the risk if AI isn’t as successful as expected.

SpaceX, Elon Musk’s rocket company that also runs the xAI business, had similar swings. It opened with a loss and then flipped to a gain of 0.4 per cent after it agreed to a roughly $US40 billion deal with an entity managed by Apollo Global Management to lease AI computing power.

Musk warned over the weekend that hundreds of companies that rent out AI computing power are under threat because of the difficulty in borrowing money, saying on his social-media platform, X, that they could face “guppy-level death and consolidation.”

Profit reports from huge tech companies this upcoming week could offer more details about how spending on AI is going. Alphabet and Microsoft will report their latest quarterly results on Wednesday, with Amazon to follow on Thursday.
They’re among the roughly one out of every three stocks in the S&P 500 scheduled to report their latest quarterly results this week.

In other international markets, Brazilian stocks fell sharply, costing the country’s richest bankers about $US9 billion after leftist President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won reelection in a result that surprised investors.

items.title: Anthropic’s record US$2 trillion stock market listing highlights the growing risks for all of us
paras: NurPhoto/Getty Images Anthropic’s record US$2 trillion stock market listing highlights the growing risks for all of us Published: October 27, 2026 1:26am EDT Anthropic, developer of AI chatbot Claude, has filed its prospectus and is expected to go public on Wall Street in November at a valuation of up to US$2 trillion.
That would make it the highest-valued initial public offering (IPO) ever, ahead of SpaceX’s US$1.77 trillion listing in June. OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, is expected to follow next year.
While these AI-powered IPOs are massive, they reflect an ever bigger trend: holding AI risk is becoming unavoidable for most investors.
How much of your portfolio depends on how well AI does? If you invest in an S&P 500 index fund, the answer is about 44% .

In addition, most of the market’s gains right now come from AI. Just six companies – Apple, Microsoft, Meta and chipmakers Nvidia, Micron and AMD – delivered 57% of the S&P 500’s gains since April. Without them, the index would have risen about 4% rather than 10%.

For investors or even future retirees, that AI exposure is already in their portfolios and pension funds. For example, at the end of 2025 Australians held nearly A$1 trillion in US shares – through superannuation or pension funds, other managed funds, and their own investments.
Normally, investors can lower their stock market risk by allocating some money to bonds, which are generally seen as safer investments.

But AI companies are now the biggest borrowers in the bond market , to help finance their massive spending needs. They have issued about US$466 billion of bonds so far this year – more than four times last year’s pace.
The five hyperscalers alone – Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft and Oracle – account for 11% of new US highly rated bonds (known as “investment grade” bonds) so far in 2026, up from 2% in 2024.
And nearly half of this year’s US$80 billion in data-centre bonds are rated as speculative grade, also known as “junk bonds”.
At first glance, big tech companies look safe. Their investment-grade ratings indicate that each individual company is unlikely to default.

But the credit ratings do not account for simultaneous defaults in case of a market-wide AI crash. If consumer and business demand for AI disappoints, tech companies’ bond prices and credit ratings would likely fall together – just as their shares would.
In addition to purely financial risks, AI poses risks of extinction akin to nuclear weapons , as some of the AI companies themselves have warned.
Increasingly, AI agents are plugged into real-world systems, from company networks to military cyber operations . Some have already escaped test environments and attacked companies .

This means that if AI agents misbehave when these systems are even more integrated with the physical world, “pulling the plug” on these systems becomes impractical, just as it is impractical to shut down the internet.

The risk of AI agents misbehaving — the “alignment problem” — is especially acute because of the race to build artificial general intelligence (AGI). Labs already use each generation of AI to help build the next: Anthropic’s prospectus says Claude now helps build the next Claude .

The widely read AI 2027 scenario, by former OpenAI researcher Daniel Kokotajlo and colleagues, sketches where this could lead: AI that automates AI research itself . This would set off a feedback loop in which each generation improves faster than humans can check it.
In this scenario, a US lab racing a Chinese rival keeps going even as its models start deceiving their engineers .
Worryingly, this same dynamic is listed in Anthropic’s own risk disclosures.
It is telling that in its prospectus filing, Anthropic dedicates about 94 of its 335 main pages – nearly 30% – to risk factors, compared with about 64 pages (19%) describing its business.

Among those risks, Anthropic lists an extraordinary warning that advanced AI could pose “ catastrophic or existential risks to humanity ”. That includes models that resist shutdown, conceal information or behave in ways resembling blackmail.
Disclosure works when investors can price a risk and choose to avoid it. Neither is true here.
A catastrophic AI failure would affect societies worldwide. And as Anthropic warns in its filing documents, the legal risk is vast . Insurers may not be able to cover the potential liability.
In economic terms, AI safety is a public good. Each lab bears only a fraction of the cost of getting it wrong, but captures the rewards of moving fast.

In the absence of government-mandated AI safety standards, companies’ investments in safety will deliver negative returns. So with market incentives alone, AI models will likely remain less safe than socially optimal, especially with the arms-race incentives that dominate now.

That leaves governments. Clear rules – mandatory independent testing before powerful models are released, and clear liability when autonomous agents cause harm – would turn voluntary pledges into legal obligations.
And because the race to gain artificial general intelligence is being run between the US and China, not just between labs, those rules will need international agreement.
AI risks are here to stay — both in financial markets and at the societal level. And managing those risks will require both governments and the private sector to participate.

items.title: Parties may have competing tax visions, but paying for NZ’s future isn’t getting cheaper
paras: Andrzej Rostek/Getty Images Parties may have competing tax visions, but paying for NZ’s future isn’t getting cheaper Published: October 26, 2026 7:43pm EDT It may be taking a back seat to cost-of-living pressures , unemployment and the state of the economy , but tax was always going to be a hot issue in this year’s election.

Labour is proposing a capital gains tax on investment property, while the Greens and Te Pāti Māori have each put forward wealth taxes. To fund its version of a universal basic income, Opportunity is advocating a bold land value tax – something both major parties have ruled out supporting.

National has promised no new taxes, while also campaigning on a claim a Labour-led coalition could introduce nine. That figure dubiously combines proposals from several potential support parties, many of which Labour has ruled out adopting. ACT is meanwhile emphasising lower taxes and policies to encourage investment.

Whatever the election outcome, the next government will face the same tough fiscal choices. It will inherit pressing spending needs across health , education and infrastructure, alongside the growing costs of an ageing population .
Meeting these demands will require difficult decisions about spending, taxation and borrowing, while also managing debt and responding to years of weak productivity growth .

The face of business – with multinationals, digital commerce and new forms of working – is quickly changing. That makes it harder for a system focused on taxing income and consumption to capture where economic value is created and ensure it is taxed fairly.
New Zealand relies heavily – arguably too heavily – on taxing personal and business income and consumption, while other forms of economic gain receive lighter or no taxation.

GST is efficient to collect but falls proportionately more heavily on lower-income households, which tend to spend a greater share of their earnings on goods and services. Meanwhile, those with assets generally have more scope to minimise their tax burden than those earning a wage or salary.
One example of the challenges facing New Zealand’s tax system has received relatively little attention during the election campaign: how we pay for transport.

Since the 2023 election, policy has started to shift away from a system that relies heavily on taxing petrol consumption – through fuel excise duty – and towards charging motorists directly for their use of the road network.

This is visible in the application of road user charges to light electric vehicles and plug-in hybrids from April 2024, followed by the removal of Auckland’s regional fuel tax . More fundamentally, the government has proposed replacing fuel excise duty with electronic road user charges for all light vehicles.
Fuel excise duty has historically worked as a proxy for road use for light petrol vehicles, with motorists paying the duty when they purchase petrol.
But as vehicles become more efficient, litres consumed – and therefore duty paid – become less reliable measures of kilometres travelled and actual road use.

Electric vehicles have also avoided fuel excise duty completely. This made sense as an incentive to encourage their adoption, but moved away from a user-pays principle. A universal road user charging system would also provide a more stable revenue base for the government.

At present , duties, levies and taxes (excluding GST) total 77.25 cents per litre of petrol. This is primarily made up of fuel excise duty, which goes into the National Land Transport Fund , at 70.024 cents per litre, and the ACC levy of 6 cents per litre, plus smaller levies.
Read more: Election Policy Tracker: your guide to what the parties are promising during the 2026 election campaign
GST of 15% comes on top, meaning the government also collects more GST as petrol prices rise.

To address cost-of-living pressures, in March 2022 the government temporarily cut fuel excise duty by 28.5 cents per litre (including GST) and reduced road user charges paid by diesel vehicles by 36%.

At that time, petrol prices had risen above $3.25 per litre in some main centres. The current government has instead cancelled a planned fuel excise increase for 2027, with the next increase deferred until 2028.

The greater shift towards road user charges illustrates a fundamental challenge: taxes designed around how people once travelled and consumed energy become less effective as technology and behaviour change.

Unless the next government is willing to borrow more, and accept the higher interest costs associated with that, it will need to reduce spending or increase taxes. Without more fundamental reform, however, the options for raising additional revenue are limited.

One option is a comprehensive capital gains tax , which would place more of the burden on those with greater capacity to pay. Whether such a tax is pursued will depend heavily on the political priorities of the next government.
But any tax proposal involves trade-offs, and parties should be clear about who stands to gain and who will pay more.

Voters should be asking how much each proposal will raise or cost, and how it will be funded. They should also know which groups will be affected, whether a new tax can be implemented and enforced without unnecessary complexity, and how it might influence saving, investment and other behaviour.
Just as importantly, parties should explain what they want their tax policies to achieve: raising revenue, changing behaviour, encouraging economic growth or some combination of these.
New Zealand needs a tax system that remains robust as technology, demographics, economic conditions and governments change.
The taxation of transport shows why reform cannot be deferred: as our economy evolves, taxes designed for the past become less effective and, eventually, less fair.
From the cost of living to how best to tackle climate change, the coming election involves some big choices.
This article is part of The Conversation’s Election 2026 series : expert analysis of the major policy debates and the big challenges New Zealand’s next government will face.

items.title: Outback mining jobs are on the rise with no workers to fill them
paras: The Queensland Resources Council warns of continued job shortages in the mining industry, without urgent action. ( Supplied: Chamber of Minerals and Energy )
Mines are set to restart in outback Queensland, opening up jobs for residents.
But a workforce shortage plagues the industry, worrying companies mining critical minerals.
The peak Queensland resources body warns it will be years before the next generation of skilled workers enters the industry.
Drilling is ramping up across the internationally acclaimed North West Minerals Province in Queensland and jobs are set to open up, but mining companies are struggling to find workers.
The region, in the state's north-west, is one of the most mineral-rich in the world, with an estimated $680 billion worth of resources.

With about 85 critical minerals projects underway in the area, coupled with further drilling, exploration and the reopening of previously closed mines, companies are concerned a shortfall of skilled workers will hamper progress.
The Capricorn Copper Mine north of Mount Isa lost crucial infrastructure during the floods. ( Supplied: 29Metals )
AIC Mines, owner and operator of the prominent Eloise copper mine, 60 kilometres south-east of Cloncurry, secured a binding agreement to acquire another north-west copper project, Mt Cuthbert.
Owned by Malaysian company Materra Metals Limited, the site had been in care and maintenance since 2022.
AIC Mines chairman Aaron Colleran said he "sees nothing but opportunity" in the Mt Cuthbert project, which AIC had been caretaking, but he said employment was an issue.
Aaron Colleran says filling employment gaps is an issue across the whole mining sector. ( Supplied: AIC Mines )
"We're very keen to have as large a percentage [of local workers] as possible, [but] we're having difficulty employing people, let alone employing people within the region."
He said hiring fly-in fly-out (FIFO) workers, based in Townsville and Brisbane, was a second preference.
The Australian Resources and Energy Employer Association reported that, by 2027, the mining industry would need 24,000 new workers to uphold new projects across the country.
Like Mt Cuthbert, operations at another major copper-silver mine near Mount Isa, which once employed about 400 workers, were set to restart by the end of the year.
29Metals CEO James Palmer said employees at the Capricorn Copper Mine were mostly locals, which was essential for the region's economy.
"The workforce predominantly came from north Queensland, both north-west and Mount Isa, but we've got a lot of our current workforce from Cairns, Townsville and Brisbane," Mr Palmer said.
Queensland Resources Council director of workforce strategy and capability Karina Lee Jones said the skills shortage was not just statewide, but across Australia.
"One of the main reasons for it is that we have competing skill needs, and a lot of these skill needs are coming from the south-east corner [of Queensland]," Ms Lee Jones said.
"There's a lot of public infrastructure build underway [including for] the Olympic Games."
The North West Minerals Province is one of the world's richest mineral-producing regions. ( Supplied: Queensland Department of Resources )
She said the largest shortages were mining engineering roles, as well as geologists, electricians and mechanical engineers.

"It's been impacting the industry … particularly for the last five years or so and we saw a drop-off of young people, particularly going into the trades and into certain mining-related careers," Ms Lee Jones said.
The Eloise Copper Mine, near Cloncurry, is another major site experiencing worker shortages. ( Supplied: AIC Mines )
She said a greater push was needed to get young people interested in the industry, but the shortage would remain while new recruits were coming through the ranks.
"We need to be telling a really good story about what the opportunities are to relocate to these regional locations or to the FIFO camps, if that's the option that is available to them."

items.title: Queensland youth advocate claims government cut budget in retaliation
paras: Katherine Hayes says her organisation has been shown to help reduce youth re-offending. ( ABC News: Chris Gillette )
Youth Advocacy Centre chief executive Katherine Hayes says the organisation has lost $3m in government funding.
The service supports young people in contact with the justice system and child safety.
The youth justice minister says YAC failed to meet the government's KPIs to reduce offending on bail.
A leading advocacy group says its funding has been slashed for criticising the Queensland government's strong-handed youth justice measures.
The Youth Advocacy Centre (YAC) provides legal services and support to young people in and around Brisbane who are in contact with the judicial system, child safety, or are homeless or at risk.
Chief executive Katherine Hayes said her organisation had applied for a swathe of tenders after their contract, set to expire in 2028, was cut short.

"That's $3 million, that's 19 frontline workers, that's 350 kids per year [who won't receive] training courses, counselling, medical assessments, housing, food, clothing, family therapy," Ms Hayes said.
Ms Hayes believes the only reason her funding has been cut is because she has been critical of the government and its approach to dealing with youth crime.

She said her organisation has "unprecedented experience" in the sector, and YAC's program had been independently reviewed by the government and shown to reduce offending "more than any other program that was in place at the time". She said YAC's performance benchmarks had always been met.

"It's hard not to be angry, particularly when you see the distress that it's caused to the young people who have long-standing relationships with our workers, and we've had kids say that without YAC, they wouldn't be here today."
Aimee McVeigh accused the government of making laws "in an echo chamber" earlier this year. ( ABC News: Michael Lloyd )
Community groups had anonymously spoken to the ABC earlier this year, saying they were effectively gagged from speaking out in fear of retribution .

The head of Queensland Council of Social Service Aimee McVeigh earlier accused the government of "making laws in an echo chamber," after the social service body was not invited to speak at public hearings to discuss proposed breach bail, go to jail laws.
The legislation is expected to pass parliament this week with bilateral support.
Youth Justice Minister Laura Gerber says reoffending on bail remains above 60 per cent. ( ABC News )

"Because in every tranche of new youth justice law that comes through, the government has received an avalanche of reliable, evidence-based submissions which show why the laws won't reduce re-offending. And they never consider those submissions."
The committee overseeing the bail law overhaul made no recommendations for change to the legislation.
Opposition leader Steven Miles said the YAC had been "LNP'd" and the funding cut was designed to send a message to other frontline services.
"They want to send a chill through other organisations and scare them off from talking to Queenslanders," he said.
"Their bail support program has been evaluated in detail and proven to work.

"The only reason to remove their funding is if you do not want an advocacy service speaking out against your government, and that's precisely why David Crisafulli has made this decision, which will affect 19 hardworking staff."
Youth Justice Minister Laura Gerber denied that YAC had met her government's performance indicators.
"The program was not renewed because it was not delivering on the Crisafulli Government’s KPIs to not offend while on bail, and reoffending remained higher than 60 per cent."

items.title: ASX wobbles despite Anthropic gains on Wall Street; Banks fall, miners rise
paras: Advertisement Updated Business Markets World markets ASX wobbles despite Anthropic gains on Wall Street; Banks fall, miners rise Staff writers Updated October 27, 2026 — 10:38am , first published 5:28am
You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

Share A A A The Australian sharemarket had a muted start to trading on Tuesday, despite a strong lead from Wall Street which had been buoyed by the IPO filing of Anthropic, a tent pole of the AI industry.

The S&P/ASX 200 was down 11.8 points, or 0.1 per cent, at 8798.10 at around 10.30am AEDT, with four of its 11 industry sectors in the red. It had added 0.2 per cent on Monday. The Australian dollar was trading at US70.15¢.
Losses by banks and consumer stocks weighed on the local market, while the mining heavyweights and the tech sector advanced on the global AI trade. Energy stocks also rose.

Anthropic’s IPO filing gave tech stocks on Wall Street a boost, and also lifted the local tech sector. Bloomberg While the price for a barrel of Brent crude slipped 0.8 per cent to $US115.81 in the morning, it remains near the high end of its range since the war with Iran began. The highest price for the fossil fuel since then is nearly $US120, reached in March.
On Wall Street overnight, US stocks climbed as investors digest Anthropic’s filing for its initial public offering and look ahead to key big tech earnings this week.
The S&P 500 rose 0.7 per cent and more than recovered its losses from last week. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 0.3 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite closed 0.8 per cent higher.
Anthropic filed for its long-awaited market float, a landmark moment in the artificial-intelligence industry that is growing ever-hungrier for cash to power ahead.

The company behind Claude expects to begin trading on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol ANT, a filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission showed. Anthropic filed confidentially in June for a listing.

Investors are telling bankers on the deal that their estimate of a fair valuation has shifted down to around $US1.4 trillion to $US1.5 trillion ($2 trillion to $2.1 trillion) after the company’s investor day, according to people familiar with the matter. A valuation of closer to $US1.75 trillion is potentially achievable, some of the people said, asking not to be identified as the information isn’t public.

Microsoft closed 1.5 per cent higher after it announced it will offer buyouts to about 60,000 workers, part of the company’s efforts to trim costs and retool its workforce for the artificial intelligence era. Some personnel in the US, Canada, India and the UK at a vice president level and below will be eligible, said a Microsoft spokesperson.

The strongest lift for the market came from Nvidia, which rose 2.4 per cent. That helped the chip company recover some of its drop from three straight losing weeks, its longest such streak since June, and maintain its position as the largest stock on Wall Street above Apple.

But stocks elsewhere in the artificial-intelligence industry remained unsettled. They’ve been swerving on worries about whether their industry’s boom is under threat because of how expensive it’s become for companies to borrow money to build data centres and buy more AI chips.
Stocks are recovering their losses from last week ahead of a number of earnings reports this week from big companies, including Amazon and Intel.

Meta Platforms bounced up and down after outlining plans to raise $US35 billion by selling stock to help pay for its AI investments. It also said it could raise another $US60 billion by selling shares of a new class of its stock once it begins trading. Meta’s stock initially dropped more than 2 per cent, but it quickly flipped to a gain and then pulled back to a loss of 1.9 per cent.

The company behind Claude expects to begin trading on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol ANT AP Meta said Nvidia, Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom have already indicated they may buy a total of $US5 billion of stock in its offering. That’s a signal of strong interest from big chip companies that stand to benefit from additional AI investments. But it also gives fuel to critics of “circular financing” who say it raises the risk if AI isn’t as successful as expected.

SpaceX, Elon Musk’s rocket company that also runs the xAI business, had similar swings. It opened with a loss and then flipped to a gain of 0.4 per cent after it agreed to a roughly $US40 billion deal with an entity managed by Apollo Global Management to lease AI computing power.

Musk warned over the weekend that hundreds of companies that rent out AI computing power are under threat because of the difficulty in borrowing money, saying on his social-media platform, X, that they could face “guppy-level death and consolidation.”

CoreWeave, a company that’s borrowed money to buy AI computing power that it rents to customers, has been at the centre of investors’ worries in recent weeks. On Monday, it dropped 5.5 per cent quickly after trading began, only to flip to a gain of 1.8 per cent by the close. Such minute-to-minute swings have become commonplace for it in recent days.

Profit reports from huge tech companies this upcoming week could offer more details about how spending on AI is going, and whether it’s producing the profits and productivity that proponents promised.
Alphabet and Microsoft will report their latest quarterly results on Wednesday, with Amazon to follow on Thursday.

Companies across all industries are under pressure to report strong growth in their profits. Expectations for big growth are what allowed their stock prices to run to records recently despite worries about high inflation, high interest rates and other concerns.
Verizon Communications fell 3.5 per cent even though it reported a stronger profit for the summer than analysts expected, as its revenue fell short of forecasts.
Roughly one out of every three stocks in the S&P 500 is scheduled to report its latest quarterly results this week.

In stock markets abroad, Brazilian stocks fell sharply, costing the country’s richest bankers about $US9 billion after leftist President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won reelection in a result that surprised investors.

Other governments around the world are also feeling pressure because of their high debt loads and worries about strained budgets. France has been at the centre of the worries recently following violent protests in the country.

But yields on French government bonds eased on Monday, and its CAC 40 stock index rose 0.8 per cent for one of the world’s better moves. Indexes also rose in other European markets following a mixed finish in Asia.
The European Central Bank and the Bank of Japan will be meeting to vote on interest rates later this week.

In the US bond market, yields fell for longer-term Treasurys. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.98 per cent from 5.00 per cent late on Friday and from more than 5.30 per cent earlier this month.

The two-year Treasury yield edged up to 4.71 per cent from 4.69 per cent late Friday. It more closely tracks expectations for what the Federal Reserve will do with overnight interest rates, and the widespread expectation is that it will say on Wednesday that it is leaving the federal funds rate alone following its latest meeting.
The Fed last month hiked the fed funds rate for the first time in three years in hopes of slowing inflation, which has remained much higher than anyone would like.

items.title: Why a big discount during Black Friday sales isn't necessarily a great deal
paras: A marketing expert says you should think about more than the advertised discount during a sale. ( ABC News: Anna Chisholm )
Cyber Monday , which typically marks the end of the sale period, is on November 30 .
It is becoming hard to miss in Australia, with competing offers vying for our attention in emails, texts, app notifications and shop windows.

Black Friday sales originated in the United States as a way for retailers to make money after Thanksgiving Day, says Sara Quach Thaichon, an associate professor in marketing at Griffith University on the Gold Coast/Yugambeh language region.
But it has now become part of the Australian retail calendar and November is "almost a whole sale season" with deals beginning weeks in advance, Dr Thaicon says.
You can expect retailers to promote offers of "up to 50 per cent off" and "up to 70 per cent off" , but most discounts fall closer to 20 or 30 per cent off , she says.
Mark Serrels, the editorial director at consumer group Choice on Gadigal land in Sydney, says the Black Friday "behemoth" is expanding every year.

But before tapping a card or clicking "buy", Mr Serrels and Dr Thaicon recommend considering the value of the purchase to you, its quality and how much you're spending — rather than just how much you are saving.
While there are savings to be made, Mr Serrels says, there are "a million different ways retailers are using Black Friday to their advantage".

"[For example], they're trying to get rid of stock. They're trying to get rid of older models. They're trying to get you hooked into giving your details so they can reach out and sell more things down the line."
Sometimes products are advertised as 50 per cent off the recommended retail price (RRP) during a promotion period, but it might normally be 40 per cent off anyway.

Sara Quach Thaichon says, "the biggest advertised discounts may only apply to a small number of products, while site-wide sales can exclude popular brands or new season items." ( Supplied: Sara Quach Thaichon )
Dr Thaicon says the percentage discount can make us feel like we've scored a bargain but "doesn't actually tell us whether the final price is good".
If it's an inferior product or something you simply don't need, you've wasted money buying it, even if it was 70 per cent off, she says.
Mr Serrels says that an expensive pre-sale RPP price does not equate to quality.
"Sometimes you might think, 'oh great, that TV is 50 per cent off', but it's a shit TV, so don't buy it," he says.
"We've had coffee machines that cost $200 that outperformed $2,000 [machines in testing]."
Dr Thaicon recommends focusing on how much you're spending and what you're getting for that money.

"Instead of looking at percentage, compare the final price across different retailers, think about the quality of the product, how long it will last and how often [you will] actually use it," she says.
Research the product and compare prices before sales begin, particularly when it comes to white goods and electronics, Dr Thaicon says.
When we don't know much about "big ticket" products we tend to use price as an indicator of quality, she says.

Electronics and appliances tend to be the "most heavily promoted categories", Dr Thaicon says, and major retailers have previously offered discounts of as much as 70 per cent off on some specific products.
Mr Serrels says you should decide on the exact product you want to buy — such as the model of TV — beforehand.
This gives you the opportunity to check reviews and the product's historical pricing.
Mark Serrels says scam sites pop up more frequently during the Black Friday sales period. ( Supplied: Choice )
Mr Serrels says to try to avoid the influence of time pressure when shopping during sales, such as "you've got four minutes to complete this transaction" or "this sale only lasts for 12 hours".
"Worst case scenario it's a scam. Best case scenario you're getting bullied into buying something you're not really 100 per cent sure you actually need."
A spokesperson for the Australian Securities and Investments Commission's Moneysmart program says to check who you are buying from.
"With an unfamiliar online retailer, look for independent reviews and make sure you are using the genuine website rather than a look-alike site," they say.
Mr Serrels cautions against embracing sales with unbridled "consumer lust".
"Don't feel like you have to buy [a product] right now. There's always another sale around the corner," he says.

items.title: Anthropic files to list on stock market in potential $US1.5tn float
paras: Investors say Anthropic could be worth a record-breaking $US1.5 trillion ($2.1 trillion) when it is listed on the Nasdaq. ( Reuters: Dado Ruvic/Illustration )
Anthropic, the AI giant behind Claude, could be floated on the Nasdaq as soon as next month, despite making a $US80 billion ($114 billion) loss in the first half of 2026.
The company has flagged the potential harm its AI models could pose to humankind.

Anthropic has disclosed steep losses and red-hot revenue growth in its US initial public offering filing, as the Claude-parent laid out its ambition to build AI systems capable of reshaping the global economy despite the high costs of developing the technology.

The prospectus highlights the AI company's rapid growth over the past year, fuelled by Big Tech's breakneck spending that has driven a rally in AI stocks while raising concerns about lofty valuations and rising debt.

The company also flagged growing risks from AI technology, underscoring concerns over its potential to cause harm which had led chief executive Dario Amodei to call for a slowdown in development of advanced models.

Anthropic's net loss in the first half of 2026 widened sharply to $US80.7 billion ($114 billion), largely due to a rise in the fair value of bonds convertible into company's shares. Revenue in this period stood at about $US16.3 billion.

The company's revenue grew a staggering 1,368 per cent in the three months ending June 30 from a year ago, but warned in the prospectus that revenue growth rate could decline over time and fluctuate from time to time.
Anthropic's chief executive Dario Amodei is among those warning about the need to limit the risks of artificial intelligence. ( AP: Markus Schreiber/File )

The IPO, which is likely to be as early as later this month, is expected to establish Anthropic, the AI lab behind the viral Claude models, as a benchmark for how Wall Street values leading AI companies, including rival OpenAI.
The IPO push comes despite a once-busy fall listing calendar thinning out as choppy markets prompt companies to delay their offerings.
Analysts said that would give Anthropic access to a deep pool of capital to fund its costly AI ambitions.

Growing investor uneasy with the debt-fuelled AI investment boom has led to a global sell-off in AI and tech stocks as they start to doubt if the trillions spent on data centres, chips and computing capacity will generate fast returns to support lofty valuations.
Increasing public opposition to data centres could limit investor enthusiasm for AI companies. ( Reuters: Hollie Adams )
Some current and prospective investors are valuing Anthropic at about $USUS1.5 trillion.

Anthropic said more than half of Fortune 500 companies and over 30 per cent of Global 2000 firms were customers generating at least $US100,000 each in revenue for the company over the 12 months ended September 30.

The IPO comes as Anthropic's own research raises concerns about advanced AI systems, which in controlled tests have shown behaviours including code sabotage, fraud assistance and information manipulation .
The findings have fuelled concerns about how companies can keep powerful AI systems under control as they race to deploy them commercially.
The ‌prospectus also highlighted risks associated with its AI models, which it said could exhibit "self-preserving behaviours", including behaviour "resembling blackmail".

"Our increasing use of AI systems to accelerate our own research and development may cause the capabilities of our models to advance more rapidly than our ability to develop, validate, and implement corresponding safety, alignment, and security measures," it said.
Anthropic will trade on the Nasdaq after the IPO closes under the ticker symbol "ANT".
The filing did not reveal the terms of its offering, including the number of shares it plans to sell and the proposed price range.
Anthropic, founded in 2021 by a team of researchers, was valued at $US965 billion in May in a funding round that drew some of the biggest names in Silicon Valley and Wall Street.

"We believe this abundance of AI will rapidly transform every sector of the global economy in ways greater than the impact of industrialisation, electricity, semiconductors and the internet," the prospectus said.
The company said it expects compute and infrastructure expenses to increase in absolute dollars and remain its largest operating expense for the foreseeable future.
Anthropic remains locked in a fierce battle with OpenAI to lead the race to build the most advanced AI systems.
The ChatGPT maker confidentially filed for an IPO in June and is expected to list by early 2027.
Anthropic's IPO follows that of Elon Musk's SpaceX, which rewrote the IPO record books in June, when it priced a $US75 billion offering that valued the company at $US1.75 trillion.

items.title: Reserve Bank holds 36 th Conference of State Finance Secretaries
paras: The 36 th Conference of State Finance Secretaries was held on October 27, 2026 at RBI, Mumbai. The theme of the Conference was ‘Role of Quality of Expenditure, Effective Cash and Prudent Debt Management in Enhancing States’ Fiscal Sustainability’. The Conference was attended by the Finance Secretaries of 27 States and three Union Territories as well as senior officials from the Ministry of Finance, Government of India, Controller General of Accounts and the Comptroller and Auditor General of India. Governor, Reserve Bank of India inaugurated the Conference. Addressing the participants, the Governor emphasised the importance of maintaining the quality of expenditure to ensure the long-term fiscal health of the States. He also emphasised on the need for the States to adopt prudent borrowing strategies and efficient cash management practices. The Governor urged the States to onboard onto the Unified Lending Interface (ULI) and utilise Programmable Central Bank Digital Currency (P-CBDC) for Direct Benefit Transfers (DBT). He also advised States to make effective use of the State Level Bankers’ Committee (SLBC) forum. During the Conference, the Governor released a Booklet titled ‘Compendium on Cash and Debt Management for State Governments’. The Booklet summarises relevant concepts, operational processes and good cash and debt management practices in a concise and accessible format. paras: Join our Whatsapp channel New Delhi [India], October 22 (ANI): The Enforcement Directorate has arrested six persons in connection with an investigation under Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA) linked to a cross-border drugs smuggling network . An investigation by the Directorate of Enforcement ( ED ) unearthed a major drug trafficking operation involving the smuggling of heroin from Afghanistan into India. Lovejit Singh alias Labba , Manjeet Singh alias Manna were arrested on October 11 while Prabhjit Singh, Gurjot Singh and Ramandeep Singh were arrested on October 18 and one Gurpreet Singh was held on October 20, the agency said in a statement. ED investigation revealed that the arrested persons ie Lovejit Singh, Manjeet Singh, Ramandeep Singh, Gurjot Singh, Gurpreet Singh and Prabhjit Singh, coordinated the smuggling, storage and distribution of heroin across Punjab, Haryana, and Delhi. They were were key members of a syndicate that smuggled heroin from Afghanistan and Iran concealing them within shipments of talc stone and gypsum powder.

According to the central probe agency the accused persons incorporated Sandhu Exports, a front company owned by Prabhjit Singh, to carry out the smuggling of drugs. According to ED , the investigation under PMLA linked to a cross-border drugs smuggling network was initiated based on the seizure of 293.81 kg of heroin from containers imported by Sandhu Exports at Nhava Sheva Port by DRI and the seizure of 352.71 kg of heroin from two vehicles and a flat in Faridabad, Haryana by the Delhi Police Special Cell. Thus, a total of 646.52 Kg. of heroin has been seized so far. ED uncovered the highly sophisticated heroin smuggling and money laundering network where the identification of multiple bank accounts, cash transactions, and operational expenses by the accused has been made. The accused disguised the origin of the illicit funds, which were further layered and integrated into seemingly legitimate financial activities. It was also revealed that the syndicate did not make any payments to Afghan suppliers until the drugs were sold in the local market. Further, the accused used cash payments to purchase multiple vehicles in the second-hand market for trafficking from the storage hubs to further distribution. The ED investigation revealed that cash was used for the purchase of high-end smartphones and encrypted communication apps were used to coordinate smuggling activities. Drugs smuggled from Iran and Afghanistan used to be imported via Nava Sheva port in Mumbai, later stored at a rented godown in Shivpuri Madhya Pradesh, and further distributed for local supply in parts of Delhi, Punjab and Haryana. Transportation was carried out in lesser quantities of 10 kg to prevent detection by law enforcement agencies. Previously, a property in Jandoli Village (Rajpura, Punjab), multiple bank accounts in the names of accused persons, and fixed deposits were attached by the ED . (ANI)

items.title: Mukka Proteins Limited Announces Rs 98 Crore Preferential Issue for Acquisition and Expansion
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel VMPL Mumbai (Maharashtra) [India], October 22: Mukka Proteins Limited , India's largest fish meal and insect meal producer and a leader in the animal protein industry , has announced the approval of a preferential issue worth Rs 98 crore by its Board of Directors. This strategic move will help Mukka Proteins in its ongoing domestic and international acquisition and expansion efforts, reinforcing its position in the global market. A significant portion of the funding will come from the promoter and promoter group, underlining their commitment to the company's robust growth strategy. The preferential issue will comprise up to 1.96 crore equity shares at Rs50 per share, aggregating to Rs98 crore. This price includes a premium of Rs49 per share on the face value of Rs1. Mukka Proteins will use the raised capital to enhance production capabilities and meet the growing global demand for sustainable and high-quality protein solutions, particularly in the fishmeal and insect meal sectors. In a clear show of confidence, Mukka Proteins' promoters have committed to a capital infusion of INR 60 crore through a preferential allotment of equity shares. This significant financial backing will be used to strengthen the company's financial position, reduce debt, and fund key operational improvements. Mukka Proteins has consistently embraced sustainability, having commercialized insect protein as a significant innovation for the aquaculture and animal feed industry. The company's waste-to-food initiatives have contributed to environmental sustainability, particularly in collaboration with the Mangaluru municipality for waste management. These efforts not only align with global environmental best practices but also enhance circular economy processes, focusing on converting municipal waste into valuable protein and oil products. Mukka Proteins is known for its strong commitment to ecological preservation, evident through the development of sustainable products such as fishmeal, fish oil, and insect protein. As a key player in the aquaculture and nutraceutical markets, Mukka contributes 25-30% of the market share in India's fishmeal and fish oil industry. The company plans to expand its operations further, capitalizing on this capital infusion to enter new markets and enhance its global footprint.

This issuance is subject to necessary statutory and regulatory approvals, including shareholder approval at the upcoming Extra-Ordinary General Meeting (EGM) on November 16, 2024. Managing Director and CEO Harris commented, "This preferential issue is a major milestone for Mukka Proteins as we continue to strengthen our market position. Our growth plans remain firmly rooted in sustainability, and this capital will enable us to scale up production, diversify our product offerings, and reinforce our commitment to responsible and eco-friendly business practices." Mukka Proteins Limited is poised to capture new opportunities in the animal protein sector, reinforcing its legacy of innovation, sustainability, and operational excellence. Mukka Proteins Limited : Mukka Proteins Limited is a leading manufacturer and exporter of fish meal , fish oil, and other protein products. The company has built a reputation for delivering high-quality, sustainable protein products to a global customer base. With a commitment to innovation and quality, Mukka Proteins serves industries including aquaculture, pet food, and agriculture across multiple continents. Headquartered in Mangalore, India, Mukka Proteins operates state-of-the-art processing facilities that meet stringent international standards. The company is dedicated to sustainable practices and has been at the forefront of environmental stewardship within the protein processing industry.
